safety.en: River paths gave me more room, while road crossings and crowds made the historic centre less suitable for regular runs.

scenery.en: The river, historic surroundings and that quiet early view towards the Colosseum made this a very memorable city run.

surface.en: Paved paths, cobblestones and changes of surface near the sights made this less uniform than a seafront promenade.

access.en: The Tiber helps connect a longer, relatively flat run, while crowds and crossings interrupt central streets.

experience.en: Knowing where to run made Rome much more enjoyable, and the quiet morning near the Colosseum remains a favourite memory.

en.title: Rome: sunrise means magic
en.excerpt: A 16 km morning run along the Tiber and towards the Colosseum, one unforgettable sunrise, post-run coffee and a dinner I still defend.

practicalSummary.goodFor: Early morning riverside runs with an optional detour towards the Colosseum.
practicalSummary.terrain: Paved riverside paths, city streets and cobblestones near the sights.
practicalSummary.keepInMind: Go early, allow for road crossings and save the crowded historic centre for walking.

en.body:
I have travelled to Rome with my running shoes twice now. From a running point of view, it immediately reminded me a little of Paris: an old city, a big river through it, and the possibility of following the water instead of weaving through every busy street.

On my first visit, I struggled a bit to find the places where running actually felt enjoyable. There were plenty of tourists, and I did not yet have a clear idea of how to connect the better stretches. The second time, I understood the city a little more and could enjoy the running much more too.

My main recommendation is simple: go early. And for a normal run, I would largely leave the old town and the busy historic centre to the people walking around them. There are enough other places to run in Rome without turning a sightseeing crowd into a slalom course. I would rather explore those streets on foot afterwards.

## Along the Tiber, then towards the Colosseum

The morning run I am sharing here was about 16 km out and back. The GPX adds up to 16.4 km including the return and the slightly different streets I used along the way.

The line links the Prati side of the city with the Tiber, follows the river south past the Castel Sant’Angelo area and along the Trastevere side, then heads inland towards Circus Maximus and the Colosseum. The return brings it back towards the river and north again. It is a useful example of how I connected a longer riverside run with one memorable early-morning detour.

The river paths were the parts where I could settle into a rhythm most easily. Around bridges and where I needed to cross roads, I still had to slow down and wait for cars. A river beside you does not mean every connection is uninterrupted, so I would leave time for those pauses rather than treat this as a perfectly continuous tempo route.

The recording has only about 40 m of accumulated climbing, with elevations roughly between 17 and 38 m. In other words, this was not a hill workout like [my Chianti run](/journal/tuscany-chianti/). There is a modest rise after leaving the riverside towards the Circus Maximus and Colosseum area, around 5 to 8 km into this recording. The surface changes and crossings were more noticeable interruptions than the climbing.

![Elevation profile of the 16.4 km Rome run, with the Tiber stretches and Colosseum area marked approximately](/assets/uploads/rome/elevation-profile.svg "16.4 km including the return, with approximately 40 m of climbing according to the GPX. Place labels and elevations are approximate.")

## One of those mornings I will remember

One moment from this run is still among my favourite running memories. I was on Via di San Gregorio, looking towards the Colosseum in the distance. It was still early, the light was only beginning to turn golden, and for that moment the road was completely empty of people and cars.

I was jogging along with my mouth practically hanging open. It felt as though I had somehow run into ancient Rome. Absolutely epic. I was so busy taking it in that I forgot to take a photo of that exact moment.

So I asked ChatGPT to create an illustration of the feeling: the quiet road, the first warm light and a glimpse of the Colosseum farther ahead. The image below is AI-generated from my memory, rather than a photograph or an exact reconstruction of the street.

![AI-generated illustration of an empty road inspired by Via di San Gregorio at early dawn, with a small view of the Colosseum in the distance](/assets/uploads/rome/via-di-san-gregorio-dawn-ai.jpg "AI-generated illustration inspired by my memory of that morning. It is not a photograph of the run or an exact street view.")

That very quiet moment was a special early-morning experience. It is not how I would describe running through central Rome in general. Once the historic streets fill up, I would choose the riverside for my run and come back to the old centre for a walk.

## Coffee, a pastry and one very defensible dinner decision

This is Rome, so food has to make an appearance. A coffee and a pastry after a run felt like a very good way to continue the morning. My photo also includes one of my favourite places to eat in the city: [Trattoria Pizzeria Luzzi](https://www.trattorialuzzi.it/), near the Colosseum.

Luzzi’s own [family history](https://www.trattorialuzzi.it/trattoria/) says it began in 1945, when Amedeo and Benilde moved their restaurant to Via San Giovanni in Laterano after the Second World War. The business has passed down through the same family. What I like about it is much simpler than any grand restaurant description: straightforward, genuine food and very good value for money.

![Bruschetta at Trattoria Luzzi beside a photo of a post-run coffee and pastry at an outdoor café table](/assets/uploads/rome/luzzi-and-post-run-coffee.jpg "Luzzi on the left; coffee and a pastry after a run on the right.")

On my last trip with friends, there was also a RÜFÜS DU SOL concert. They are one of my favourite artists, but Luzzi had its usual long queue and packed tables. Since we were travelling as a larger group, getting a table at the trattoria was particularly difficult, especially with its walk-in-only system. So when I saw a chance to go there on my own, I took it. Unfortunately, that meant sacrificing the concert. My friends still occasionally make fun of me for choosing a trattoria over RÜFÜS, and in a parallel universe, I would probably regret missing that concert a lot. In this one, I stand by my decision. :)

## Run clubs and group runs

I have not joined these groups myself yet. These are options I found while putting the story together, checked in November 2026. Confirm the latest meeting point, time and any joining requirements with the organisers. The two parkruns are weekly community 5Ks rather than conventional clubs.

### Runners of Rome

A social running community whose [own website](https://www.runnersofrome.com/) says workouts are free, but you must request a place through their app first. The current dates and meeting points are in the app rather than a fixed timetable I could verify; they also ask that you can already run for at least 40 minutes. [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/runners_of_rome/).

### Amor Run Club

Weekly social runs, including an easy 5K, with an emphasis on meeting people and spending time together afterwards; the [club’s website](https://amorrunclub.com/) points to Instagram for the current day and start details. [Local coverage lists the regular run as free](https://secretroma.com/en/groups-for-running-rome/), but check the latest event for any charges or sign-up requirements, especially for the social part afterwards. [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/amor_runclub/).

### Roma Road Runners Club

A more traditional athletics club with a community around road running and the city’s parks. Its [published programme](https://www.romaroadrunnersclub.it/images/documents/PRESENTAZIONE_ATTIVITA_RRRC_2024-2025.pdf) includes free Sunday group training; because that document covers 2024/25, I would [contact the club](https://www.romaroadrunnersclub.it/) to confirm the next session open to visitors rather than assume the old timetable still applies. Membership and structured courses are separate from those advertised free sessions.

### Caffarella parkrun

A free weekly 5 km run, jog or walk in Parco della Caffarella, with a community atmosphere and no need to chase a fast time. The [park’s own information](https://www.caffarella.it/il-parco/) lists Saturday at 09:00 near Largo Pietro Tacchi Venturi; use the [event page](https://www.parkrun.it/caffarella/) for registration, the exact course and any cancellations.

### Roma Pineto parkrun

Another free Saturday community 5K, this time in the Pineto park area, with room for runners and walkers at their own pace. The [organisers’ Strava listing](https://www.strava.com/clubs/438137/group_events/292723) gives 09:00 on Saturday and Via Vittorio Montiglio; check the [official event page](https://www.parkrun.it/romapineto/) before going and register with parkrun first.

If you run with a group in Rome and something here should be changed, added or removed, please let me know on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/markuskaljuste/) or [Strava](https://strava.app.link/W1a7SCITG7b). I would much rather keep the information useful than pretend I have tried every club myself.
